Extra colours

Violet costs 25 points per square: 50 for a paired country, 25 for the single square. This is a fixed rule. Further colours cost five times the previous colour: 125, 625, and so on.

Pairing uses search, with exact endgame analysis when time permits. Completed maps use an exact minimum-penalty solver.

What counts as solved?

Search estimates guide exploration. Exact final colourings establish facts. A position is marked proven only when rigorous lower and upper bounds meet, accounting for every distinct legal reply that matters. Already formed countries also give a guaranteed minimum penalty. A solved continuation can establish a bound for its parent; one good-looking line cannot prove an opening.

The book merges rotations, reflections, country renaming and different pairing orders. General graph equivalence is not used yet. Imported labels are ignored: final colourings and proof implications are recomputed.

A SEPARATE LEARNING ENGINE

Gomulda Zero

Learn through self-play or practise against Gomulda Search in both roles.

Gomulda Search · unchangedGomulda Zero · experimental

A neural network learns which pairs to explore and how costly a position may become. Its search generates new games; their exact colouring penalties become training targets.

One network, two roles

White pairs first and tries to make the final colouring expensive. Black pairs second and tries to keep it cheap. The network receives the current role at every position, including after the players swap sides.

How the role is encoded

A dedicated input is +1 for White and −1 for Black. Training values are +penalty ÷ 10 for White and −penalty ÷ 10 for Black. Search maximizes White’s penalty and minimizes it for Black. The player’s seat number does not determine this input.

Play→Learn→Evaluate→Repeat

Training runs on this device while this page is open. Completed training is saved here. More games or lower training loss do not, on their own, establish stronger play.

The test plays eight paired matches from held-out openings, with equal time per move. Each engine gets both roles. Test games never update the network or enter its training data.

Strength test

No local test yet. Gomulda Search remains the default.

How this differs from a large AlphaZero project

This is a compact policy/value network with PUCT search, legal-move masking, exploration noise, replay, board-symmetry augmentation and gradient updates. It is a working research engine, not a claim of expert or superhuman strength. A larger model and much longer, carefully evaluated training may be needed.

Self-play retains the AlphaZero-style loop. Training against fixed Search is an opponent-training variation: Zero learns from its own decisions and the outcomes of those games, without copying Search’s moves.

Colouring stays exact in both engines. Gomulda Zero learns the pairing phase. The model uses the fixed game rules, including 25 points per square for the sixth colour.

ORIGINS & RECOLLECTIONS

The story of Gomulda

Personal recollections by Søren Riis

A name for many games

My friend Cristoffer Crone invented Gomulda around 1974. He invented many original games, and several shared the name Gomulda, including games known as 5 × 5 Gomulda and Elastik Gomulda.

The country-pairing and colouring game played here became the most popular of these inventions. Its players shared one board, with White trying to make the countries difficult to colour and Black trying to make them easier.

Mathematics and university life

When I was still in high school, Cristoffer was working on his master’s thesis. He was a fantastic source of mathematical knowledge for me.

I enjoyed parties at Elers’ Kollegium and Regensen, two prestigious student residences in Copenhagen. I later lived at Regensen myself.

Cristoffer gave me the confidence to occasionally skip high school, take the train to Copenhagen, and sit in on lectures at the University of Copenhagen. Meanwhile, the red marks and warnings for my absences accumulated at school.

Dansk Gomulda Laug

Together with Cristoffer, we founded Dansk Gomulda Laug, a small association of about 20 members. We played the game and maintained our own ratings.

I recall that my rating, around 93, was by far the highest. The other players’ ratings ranged from the low 60s to the high 70s. Curiously, our beloved Cristoffer, the game’s inventor, always had one of the lowest ratings.

Laug means “guild” or “association” in English.

THE INVENTOR

Cristoffer Crone

Date to be confirmed

Cristoffer played chess first at Gentofte Chess Club and later at Espergærde Chess Club.

He began studying mathematics at the University of Copenhagen in 1971 or 1972; I am not sure which year. His master’s thesis was about topological spaces.

Remembering a friend

Looking back, I would describe Cristoffer as markedly neurodivergent. I recall that some people speculated about schizophrenia; these were other people’s impressions. To us, Cristoffer was simply a wonderful weird person.

I also remember that Cristoffer’s differences became harder to navigate as he grew older.

The original rating system

Our rating system used the score margin of a complete two-round match. A player’s expected margin was the difference between the two ratings, divided by 10. The rating then changed by the difference between the actual and expected margins.

Expected margin = (your rating − opponent’s rating) ÷ 10

New rating = old rating + actual margin − expected margin

Both adjustments use the ratings from before the match. The two players gain and lose equal amounts.

A DRAW THAT CHANGES THE RATINGS

80 versus 70, ending 2–2

The 80-rated player is expected to win by (80 − 70) ÷ 10 = 1 point. A 2–2 draw has a margin of 0, so that player scores one point below expectation and loses one rating point. The other player gains one.

THE RULES OF

Gomulda

A game invented by Cristoffer Crone.

1. Build the countries

White chooses two empty squares for country 0. Black chooses two for country 1. Alternate through country 11. Any two empty squares can be paired, including neighbours. The last square automatically becomes country 12.

2. Black colours the map

Both squares of a country share one colour. Different countries sharing a side must have different colours; diagonals do not count. An internal border within one country is harmless. Black can revise colours freely before submitting a valid complete map.

Blue, green and yellow are free. Red costs 1 per square; black costs 5 per square. Violet, the sixth colour, costs 25 per square: 50 for a paired country, or 25 for the single square. Further colours cost five times the previous colour. These costs are fixed game rules. The total is White’s score.

3. Swap roles

Start on a fresh board with roles reversed. Each player scores once, as White. The higher score wins; equal scores are a draw.

Planning & assistance

Planning colours are erasable notes during pairing. They have no effect on legality or score and are cleared when colouring starts. Suggestions and “Let AI play” are optional help. In local two-player mode, both players share this screen.
